title: Culture Through Tension: Leading Interdisciplinary Teams with Nick Gillian

segments.text: In mobile application security, good
enough is a vulnerability. Guardsquare
delivers the highest level of security
for your mobile apps without compromise.
Discover how Guardsquare provides
industryleading security for your
Android and iOS apps at guardsquare.com.
Good day folks. This is Shane Hasty for
the InfoQ Engineering Culture Podcast.
Today I'm sitting down with Nick
Gillian. Nick, welcome. Thanks for
taking the time to talk to us today.
>> Thank you, Shane. Great to be here.
>> So, my normal starting point with these
conversations is who's Nick?
[laughter]
>> Great question. So, I'm Nick. I am the
co-founder and CTO of Archetype. We are
a physical AI company based in Palo Alto
in California, although we have teams
all throughout the US and Europe. And I
am at heart someone who has been working
on machine learning and sensing my whole
career. I really love working with
machine learning and AI and solving deep
sensor problems. I've been at archetype
for the last few years since we founded
the company. But before that I was at
Google for almost a decade where I was
running AI machine learning teams doing
a lot of ondevice sensing. Before that I
worked at Samson research and ran my own
consulting company. And then before that
I was in academia for a long time. I did
my PhD in machine learning and real-time
sensing way back in you know the early
2000s before machine learning was cool
and everyone was working on it. And then
I was at MIT for multiple years where I
did a postto there. So yeah, for almost
20 years now I've been working on
machine learning and sensing and yeah
I've really loved that life.
>> What's special about physical AI?
>> The way we would define it as a company
is we really think about any use case
where you have some form of sensor in
the world and you want to make sense of
it, right? So you want the intelligence
to take data from those sensors. It
could be cameras. It could be
microphones. It could be more kind of
temperature and electrical sensors in a
large industrial machine, for example.
It could be really complex sensors like
radar and LAR. And even you can use
Wi-Fi, for example, as a sensor, right?
You can actually turn that into a
sensing mechanism. Taking in all of
those different sensors, having a large
intelligence that can fuse that together
and kind of perceive, reason, and act,
and then be able to control that in some
output form. So that could be through
robotics to control and actuate a
system. It could be to alert a user for
example in a safety use case that you
know one of their team has climbed up
the roof of the building to power hose
it and the person managing the building
should pay more attention you know for
safety reasons or it could be at the end
of every day generating an automatic
report to say how productive your
factory was for example. So any use case
where you want to take sensing data and
you want to make sense of it and that's
really what we're working on at
archetype and I've worked on many
versions of this throughout my career.
>> This is the engineering culture podcast.
What makes a good culture?
>> Oh that's a great question for me. I
think the thing that makes a positive
culture and at least the teams that I
really enjoy to work in is when there's
a positive tension in the team between a
couple of different aspects. Right? So
for example, I really like working and
building and growing teams where there's
some form of highly ambiguous novel form
of research or innovation that you're
then trying to pull into an actual
product, right? not just do research for
research sake and write a paper and go
to a conference, but how do you actually
take that technology and bring it zero
to one, but then actually make it into a
real piece of technology that can go
into a product and then actually make
that product into hopefully multiple
products and you know a lot of the
things I've done in the past is taking
that stuff and platformize it for
example. So there's one example there
where you have the tension between
building a team that can do really
innovative research and a team that has
the rigor and the kind of methodology to
turn that into a robust product. And
there's a friction between these two
things because normally the type of
person that can like do really kind of
zero to one like inventions.
Some of the skills you need to be really
good at that are the inverse of the
skills you need to be a, you know,
engineer that can build a system that
has, you know, five nines of support and
the speed at which you work and the
rigor at which you work. There's always
a friction between those. So, I really
like that type of tension. I really like
teams where you can build a tension
between having, for example, engineers
and designers that are in the same team
or software engineers and hardware
engineers that work really closely
together to actually co-design the
hardware. So I really like these teams
where you can actually build that type
of expertise and tension in the same
team and a lot of companies the way they
do this is those different components
they sometimes live in like physically
different buildings or physically
different parts of the world and it's a
bit more waterfall. The hardware team
will build some hardware and spec it and
they'll hand it off to a software team
which will build it and spec it and
they'll hand it off to a design team
which will then put some nice layer on
top of it and that works for some
companies but I actually really like
companies that try to put everyone in
the same sub team and like build these
full stack teams. It brings in some
interesting challenges in terms of how
do you handle those different
personalities and everything else. But I
fundamentally think it leads to better
innovation, better products, more
exciting teams to work in because I can
learn a bunch of things from a hardware
expert or the way a designer thinks
about how to communicate ideas.
Sometimes I really love to kind of
absorb that. So that's the type of
culture and team I like to work in and
build and be surrounded by.
>> How do you keep that crossf functional
tension productive?
Well, I think there's not one answer to
this because I think as different
projects go through different phases
like the different life cycle of an
invention for example or the different
life cycle of a product right from the
initial kind of whiteboarding and
sketching to maybe the early prototype
to like maybe the pre-production system
to the thing you've launched to then the
thing you're going to maintain and
continually update. I think how that
tension, how that team building, how the
dynamics work is very different as the
team naturally grows over those stages
as well. How do you clearly communicate
across those teams, right? How do you
set it up so that in a twoe sprint for
example, you can actually clearly define
a goal that a designer and a hardware
engineer can work at the same speed
because takes a lot longer to kind of
build a chip than to draw a chip for
example, right? So naturally of the
progression of a project I think these
things will actually change and evolve
there's not one solution there's maybe
five or six different phases of that
life cycle right
as the team evolves through that life
cycle what's happening to the team
membership you mentioned the person
who's great at 0ero to one is not
necessarily great at the 100 to 1
million but we don't want to lose them
>> yeah yeah for Sure. So I think typically
you're going to start out with ideally
one key representative of each of those
functions, right? You're going to have
your engineering representative, maybe
someone who's going to do more of the
R&D work, maybe a person who's more
driving things from more of the design
perspective, and you want to have
ideally the smallest footprint of the
team possible because that's when you
can move fastest, right? And ideally,
you want to go through lots of ideas
quickly and throw away most of them. And
I'm a big believer that some of this
kind of innovative work, it's very hard
to like sit down and think of what the
thing is first and then go and build it.
You kind of have to get a very rough
foggy idea of the concept and then you
actually by building it, you learn what
it is, right? Particularly for some of
the things we're doing at the company
now involves a lot of multimodal output
in these models and there's not a lot of
work in that space. So we it's like even
to us it's unclear what's possible you
know what the model can possibly do and
the only way we can really work that out
is by building small prototypes and
ideas and moving very quickly and only
then we're when we're kind of all
standing around you know this box on a
Friday to do the review of like here's
the current demo only then will someone
say something be like oh that's really
good we never caught that detail and
then we can build on that and if you do
that for many many weeks and months you
remove that ambiguity and then you you
realize what this thing is that you've
been building for six months and then at
that point it becomes very obvious what
it is and very simple to define it but
it was not simple to define it maybe 6
months or 12 months before when you
started right so only by the process of
building this can you do it so as you go
through that process the team will
naturally grow from maybe those three or
four key people at the start to like
okay well now we need this real time
latency reduced as much as possible well
let's bring in an expert in system
optimization ation or in streaming or in
distributed computation or something,
right? And then you're going to start to
like maybe then build up a team and a
sub team and these people will start to
work together. So as we go through that
process, the team will naturally grow in
scope and then at some part you're going
to have to have not everyone can be in
the room at the same time, right? So
maybe now you have the lead of the team
or the manager of the team as the person
that's representative and then you have
to deal with all these communication
things of like well how do you take that
information and communicate that back to
the rest of the team who can't be there
maybe either because they're physically
in a different time zone or maybe just
they're working on another project at
the same time and they can't be in both
meetings at once for example and how do
you then capture that communication of
this is where we're going right so
there's typically um these step
functions where you build a process and
that process really starts to work and
it works for a certain point up to say
you know 20 people and then you just get
to the point where like you just can't
communicate anymore with that process
and you have to then bring in a little
bit more process and go to a new step.
that maybe brings you to say 50 people
and then at some point you just find
that like that fundamentally breaks very
quickly and then for you to go from 50
to 100 it's a very different process and
you need a lot more rigor you need a lot
more structure you need a lot more
independent slack channels and you know
documents and gits to review things as
you go through this you naturally kind
of hit these scaling barriers and each
scaling barrier you you have to say okay
it's time now to go to the next level of
process or the next level of detail you
know, to make this start to work again
cuz we we've got too big. And that will
work for x number of weeks, months,
years, and then you'll hit that scaling
limit and you'll have to go back and
review it again.
>> So, while that's going on in parallel,
how do you get the next idea at the 0ero
to one stage? Part of this is maybe not
even getting the next idea, but like
coming up with lots of ideas is
typically not the problem. Particularly
for people who work in a zero to one
area and are comfortable working there.
Ideas are, you know, dime a dozen,
right? It's uh one of the problems is
actually having too many ideas and how
do you either start to group them
together to actually come up with the
theme that unites all of those ideas and
then you can start to work on that
abstract theme as opposed to a very
specific instance of it. Or the other
one is just frankly like being able to
look at those ideas and then say which
is the idea we should prioritize first
which is going to move the needle the
most. typically there at least in my
current company and I should mention
that I co-founded it with four other
co-founders. We all worked at Google
together for almost 10 years. So we've
worked together for a long time and
we're kind of a full stack team. We have
myself in the ML and we have Jimmy who
does more of this kind of sensing work
and we have Leo who's kind of our key
designer and we have Brandon who's
really good at you know driving forward
teams and making sure things can
actually ship and then we have a van our
CEO really good at the glue to unite all
those things together right so we have
this full stack team and when we have
all these ideas we could pick it takes a
little bit of courage to try and pick
the hardest idea
because that's normally the one that
will move the needle the most even if
it's the most difficult And then you
have to be like, okay, well, there's no
way we can do this in one step. How do
we break this down into like a few
smaller steps and then maybe in one
month be able to like actually make
progress on that as opposed to taking
the most obvious, easiest thing, but
like that's probably the thing that
everybody else is going to try first.
And sometimes you try that and you maybe
get to the second or the third step of
this and you actually then realize
there's a better idea that was there all
along that you never were able to and
you can pivot and you can then go 180
degrees in a slightly more interesting
direction or maybe a direction that you
actually realize, oh actually if we did
this the customer market is much bigger
or our ability to kind of execute this
and get it into a a product, we could do
this way faster. Let's go this direction
instead.
Culture is the combination of all the
behaviors that happen. How do you keep
culture not necessarily consistent but
aligned as the organization is growing?
>> The way I typically like to think about
culture is culture is an everyday thing
in a company as opposed to some slide
deck with three words written on it. The
way I try to think about culture and I
try to actively drive this is culture is
the behaviors you amplify and it's the
behaviors you tolerate. So on the
positive side it's the things that
people do a certain way of thinking or a
certain piece of creativity or a certain
ability to be brave and take a big risk.
Those are the things you want to amplify
in a company. On the flip side of that
there's like the bad behaviors which
you're going to tolerate. And if you
know someone oversteps that line,
ideally what you want to do is call them
out on that or maybe pull them aside in
a smaller meeting or a onetoone and say
like the way you spoke to that person is
not how we think about things at this
company or the point you made was really
good but actually the way you expressed
it you completely lost the point. People
didn't capture it because they got
caught up too much in how you brought it
up. So actually why don't next time you
try to like do it this way instead of
saying person X didn't do this you bring
it up it's like we as a company are not
great at X wouldn't it be good if we
tried to do Y instead for example right
I typically find people will listen a
lot more and it's a lot more kind of an
inclusive and a supportive culture if
you do that type of thing so that's how
I think about culture it's like that
everyday behaviors that are happening in
the company and like it naturally then
flows to everybody else in the and you
have to keep an eye on it.
>> I know from our conversation earlier
before we started is that you do quite a
lot of mentoring for folks within your
own organization and outside. What's it
take to be a good mentor?
>> One things is perhaps making a lot of
mistakes yourself and putting them in
some memory bank. So if someone talks to
you, you can recall that and they don't
necessarily have to live that mistake.
That's that's maybe one thing. Another
one is starting to see as people go
through their career journey, I think
this goes back to that kind of scaling
pipeline I talked about as well. They
have a certain process that maybe works
well for them that brings them from a
low performing senior engineer to a high
performing senior engineer for example.
But the thing I realized is that some
engineers don't realize that to go from
a high performing senior engineer to a
high performing staff engineer or a
principal or to go to a director or
these you don't just keep continuing
that same behavior as a linear function
right there. There's actually specific
things at each of those stages that you
need to change or you need to really be
aware of. The way I normally phrase this
to engineers that I'm trying to mentor
and grow is as you go through your
career growth, it's about going from
doing a good job to having high impact.
For example, for a junior engineer who's
starting, for them to be good at their
job, they just need to come in and take
a task and execute the task well and
like complete the tasks on time. That's
like the bare minimum. And then as they
grow in their career, they will start to
move up to a more senior engineer. It's
like, well, instead of someone else
setting the task, you should be able to
kind of own the project and work out
what the tasks are yourself and make
sure the tasks get done. So, the project
is a good project. But then as you grow
beyond that, it's not just completing
the project, but can you actually come
out with some specific key result in
that project? Maybe you're getting
state-of-the-art compression results or
you were able to get some business
impact that you know reduce costs by 10x
or grew customers by 30x or whatever
that might be. But then the thing I see
where folks struggle to maybe go from
like that senior to staff or staff to
senior staff is going from having good
results to actually having impact of
those results to be able to communicate
those results and actually get that out
across a business or communicate those
results for example to your customers.
Maybe you have reduced customer costs by
10x for example and that's a great
internal engineering result but do your
customers know that if they come to you
they're going to get a 10x reduction in
saving right so the difference between
going from results to impact for example
I see people getting stuck on that and
typically get good result you need
really good engineering skills and
product management skills all these
things but to go from good results to
good impact that's normally where you
actually need a lot of strong soft
skills as well. So it's not just being
like the best engineer on the team or
the ability to be a very strong manager
and pull together four or five people or
20 people. It's like how do you actually
take that and then have the soft skills
to be able to go and share that with
your stakeholders or your leadership or
your customers or go and work with the
person that you know updates the website
and put that we can save you 10x in GPU
costs for example and that actually
having that as one of the key business
ROIs, right? And then I think one of the
most challenging steps is to go from
having high impact to having high
influence. That's probably one of the
most difficult things as either a very
senior engineer, a principal engineer
for example or a very senior leader like
a director or a VP. It's like can you
actually influence an entire team or an
entire org of people to go in a certain
direction with you before you even have
any results yourself. Right? they kind
of have to believe in you. You have to
be able to articulate a vision to them
or a clear goal that like is exciting or
motivating for the team or the company.
And can you actually help guide all
these people that may not even report to
you, right? They may not be in your
reporting. They may may be in different
teams or different orgs, maybe even
different companies in some case. Can
you have enough influence over these
teams to actually motivate them and get
them to want to come and work on this
project with you to then go through all
those steps again to actually get high
impact. So I think going from being good
at these kind of micro tasks to owning
projects to getting results to having
impact to having influence. I think this
step function is something I typically
help a lot of engineers first of all
just see that step function. Maybe they
don't even think about the difference
between doing a good job on a project
and actually having a key business
result coming out of it. Or it's like
this is really good work, but you
haven't had impact on it, right? So
you're missing that impact.
>> So that's a very very clear
journey that you've laid out for the
individual contributor. What are the
bumps in the road that they're going to
most likely come across? I think this is
going to really depend on which of those
stages they're at because some of those
bumps in the road are going to be
engineering challenges that require
maybe a single IC or a manager who's
managing a small team of you know four
or five engineers to be able to sit down
and say okay we're not getting the
throughput we need for this system for
example we need to completely redesign
IO infrastructure or move from pub some
sub to some or architecture design to be
able to remove this bottleneck and go
and execute it and it's you know they
can kind of control their own destiny of
like okay well let's come up with this
better design and we can go and execute
it and I can go and solve this problem
but at a certain point ability to solve
that bump in the road gets beyond your
own control to solve it and that's where
the soft skills come in where you need
to be able to go and work with for
example the database team who maybe
don't report to you or maybe are not
even in like your manager's manager's
org path and you need to be able to go
and work with them and say like we have
this really important project or
customer over here and we need to reduce
latency by X and for that we need your
team to go and implement this new
protocol or this new design to allow us
to do that because you're the owners of
that part of the system. So I think that
the bumps in the road will depend on are
they engineering bumps or are they more
cultural bumps across the company in
terms of how the speed or the process or
how people think about value for example
or priorities or they could be more of
these more team soft skills where you
either have to work closely with a
customer or another stakeholder or
another part of the company to convince
them and motivate them to kind of help
you do your job so you can like push
through that bump. Yeah. So I think as
folks go through that those step
functions as you mentioned the natural
curve of this is things go from hard
engineering problems to hard social
problems and that's really like as a
more senior manager or as a more senior
IC where you have to really start to
bring on those other skills to be able
to balance that.
>> What's the really important question I
haven't asked you?
>> Well the first question people always
ask me is where is my accent from? But
um uh that's maybe more of a sideline as
a New Zealander. Can you guess? I'm not
sure. Maybe you read my bio, so maybe
you can already guess that.
>> I didn't actually look at where you're
from, but I'm gonna guess Ireland.
>> You're very, very close. Yes, I grew up
in Northern Ireland in the UK. So, yes,
with almost 15 years here in the US, so
it's a little bit of a mix. I guess one
question you didn't ask me is maybe on
the building new products, how to handle
that ambiguity. Maybe that's a good
question. Maybe we could discuss that a
little bit.
>> Let's dig into that ambiguity.
Yeah, there's two ways I think about
handling ambiguity.
One is from more of an engineering
architectural team design perspective
and one is a lot more from a team
composition perspective. We could
briefly talk about each of those because
I think they they also support each
other. So to talk about the team
cultural perspective first I mentioned
earlier that one of the teams I really
like to work in and the type of teams
and orgs and companies I I I really like
to build are interdisciplinary teams
where you have a designer and an
engineer and a researcher and a hardware
person for example right so you're
probably familiar with like the concept
of a of a T-shaped person like a team of
you know four or five people who are all
tea in nature where they're experts in
one specific area but they can also
spill out into other key areas and
communicate clearly with someone that is
not an expert in their area. Right? The
way a hardware engineer for example
thinks about solving a problem versus a
designer versus a machine learning
engineer versus someone who's coming
more from a signal basis. the way they
look at the same problem is normally
from very different lenses.
And one of the best approaches I've seen
over you know many many products and
projects is to get like those three or
four or 10 or 20 how many people it is
voices in the same room to really start
to try and look at that problem from
different angles. And normally there's
never one angle that solves a problem.
It's normally actually to take the
through line between two or three of
them and have some form of um bottoms up
engineering solution and then top down
design solution that you kind of meet in
the middle. It's like how far can we
push the engineering to kind of solve
this problem and then how much
constraints can we put on this from a
user interaction perspective for
instance where it actually makes the
engineering problem solvable and then
normally there's very small interaction
point between how far you can stretch
the engineering and the limits of the
constraints where like that's actually
where the solution space lives right and
it can take some time as we talked about
to kind of explore that space and really
see what that angle is, but normally the
only way I've been able to ship a lot of
these very new R&D type of things and
get them into production is to work very
closely with designers to help put those
constraints on the system so you can
actually ship it. Right? In other
companies I've worked in, this is
typically where I see a lot of really
good innovative R&D. It never ships
because normally the R&D is done in one
part of the company and then it's
physically handed off to another team
and there's a big gap of death in
between that handoff and then that team
is normally a pre-production team and
then maybe they hand it off again to
like the actual team that will ship it
and again there's another gap of death
there. If you don't have all those teams
work together from the start it normally
doesn't work right. So that's one
aspect. The other aspect is and this is
maybe thinking more of an engineer is
like as a software engineer I like
abstraction a lot. I like you know clear
block diagrams a lot. They really help
me think about how to design a system or
solve a problem. And one of the things
that I find particularly with building
block diagrams, not to design the
architecture of a system, but actually
to help structure the whole team or the
project or the company is can you break
that down into maybe three, four, five
major components and then say, okay,
well the IO of each of these components
is going to be X and Y. And that
actually means that well not only can we
kind of define the kind of whole steel
cable of this you know product for
example or this project or this feature
but now it's going to work on this first
section can actually now separate that
from the second section for example and
it doesn't really matter how you're
going to go and solve part A versus part
B. We can kind of treat those as black
boxes for now as long as we can say well
the output of box A is going to be X and
then that means the input to box B is
going to be X. So just assume you're
going to get that and now can you go and
solve your problem there right? One of
the tools I liked a lot that we used to
use back at Google and we pulled the
through nacho archetype is this concept
of building we used to call it building
a steel cable right so you know when you
build a bridge for example across a
river the first thing you're going to do
is like put in those like major pillars
in the middle of the river for example
right and I typically think of those as
the API definitions for example or the
function calls to your class or
something like this here and then what
you want to do next is you want to
thread this steel cable from one side of
the river through those pillars to the
other and now you can actually start to
move buckets of concrete and nails and
other things from one side of the river
to the other and start to build the
bridge around a steel cable. So from a
product perspective it's like can you
get that initial data packet that would
come from a client to go to your
software server that then goes to some
AI model for example that then goes into
some interface that then goes back to
the client as a response. Can you think
about what those kind of key areas are
and then mock each of those components
so already from early in the project you
can get data in and data out even if
it's garbage but you can actually have
the team start to build these different
components around it and as you do that
the ambiguity of what the product is and
how it's going to work and how you're
going to solve these components the fog
of war starts to be removed I used it a
lot in my kind of early IC work to
design systems but I find it's really
helpful to actually structure teams and
like try to lead and guide projects is
to build it into these layers of
abstraction and then allow one part of
the team to go and tackle area A and one
part to tackle area B and they would
come back every day or every couple of
days and say here's the progress we've
made and that's a great way to kind of
decouple those dependencies and allow
people to kind of work in parallel.
>> Well, Nick, a lot of interesting stuff
there. If people want to continue the
conversation, where can they find you?
The best place to reach out to me is on
LinkedIn. Yeah, you just search for Nick
Gillian on LinkedIn. You'll see me. I
should be one of the first names that
pops up. Yeah,
